medical.title: Using birding to improve stroke outcomes
medical.summary: On the wooded University of Montana campus, resident Cooper's hawks are helping people recover from stroke.

medical.title: Years of fine-particle pollution track with childhood ADHD rates across US counties
medical.summary: Air quality across the country has improved greatly over the decades, as shown in Environmental Protection Agency reports. These improvements are good news overall, but lingering effects of past air pollution still raise health concerns for many people. UT researchers Alex Bentley and Larisa Ozeryansky co-authored a paper published in September in Scientific Reports. It explores the strong association between measures of fine-particulate air pollution (called PM 2.5) in the United States and the prevalence of attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) in children years later.

medical.title: Adding neurons may keep improving visual signals despite shared noise, analysis predicts
medical.summary: Our brains internally represent the outside world through the coordinated activity of billions of neurons. A single neuron responds unreliably: Even when the same stimulus is shown repeatedly, its activity varies from trial to trial. Neuron populations can compensate for this variability by representing the same information across many neurons, a strategy known as population coding.

medical.title: What is trauma‑informed care—and how do schools do it?
medical.summary: Trauma-informed approaches have become increasingly prominent in education policy and guidance, although the term is not always explicitly used.

medical.title: Hidden E. coli survive in bladder cells, but existing drug helps antibiotics reach them in lab tests
medical.summary: Urinary tract infections, or UTIs, are among the most common bacterial infections and are caused mostly by the uropathogenic bacterium Escherichia coli. But even after antibiotic treatment, many patients experience another UTI.

medical.title: New brain tumor test could transform diagnosis and treatment
medical.summary: Scientists and doctors at Newcastle are among the first in the U.K. to use a pioneering brain tumor test with the potential to speed up diagnosis for patients—from weeks to hours.

medical.title: Dietary supplement may influence lung tumor growth differently in females and males
medical.summary: A study led by researchers at the UCLA Health Jonsson Comprehensive Cancer Center found that a dietary form of a naturally occurring molecule called calcium alpha-ketoglutarate, or Ca-αKG, reduced lung tumor growth in female mice and activated genes associated with better outcomes in women with lung cancer. The researchers also found that Ca-αKG had the opposite effect in male mice, where it was associated with larger tumors and increased tumor-cell proliferation.

medical.title: Migraine and sleep are strongly interconnected, study finds
medical.summary: Sleep problems are significantly more common among people with migraine than among those without headaches. People with migraine also tend to have a later chronotype, meaning they tend to fall asleep and wake up later and are most active later in the day.

medical.title: A brainstem signal reorganizes the neural code for taste
medical.summary: Why might food seem appealing in one state of mind and less enticing in another? New UConn research offers insight into how the brain systems that regulate alertness and stress may reshape how taste is represented in the brain.

medical.title: CDC vaccine policy recommendations grind to a halt under Health Secretary Kennedy
medical.summary: The Food and Drug Administration recently approved a new flu vaccine that tested well in older adults. But the federal agency responsible for telling doctors and the general public how to use it has made no recommendation on it.

medical.title: Study identifies two factors that may help patients benefit from off-the-shelf CAR T-cell therapies
medical.summary: Researchers at The University of Texas MD Anderson Cancer Center have traced how off-the-shelf chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T cells behave in patients, revealing how immune rejection and differences among CAR T cells influence their ability to multiply after infusion.

medical.title: UACR, UPCR provide indistinguishable prognostic information in chronic kidney disease
medical.summary: In a cohort of patients with chronic kidney disease (CKD), urinary albumin-creatinine ratio (UACR) and urinary protein-creatinine ratio (UPCR) provide clinically indistinguishable prognostic information for kidney and cardiovascular outcomes, according to a research letter published online Sept. 23 in the Journal of the American Medical Association.

medical.title: Radiotherapy after surgery significantly reduces atypical meningioma recurrence, clinical trial finds
medical.summary: Atypical meningiomas are tumors that originate in the meninges and are associated with a high risk of recurrence. Until now, it was unclear whether patients benefit from radiotherapy after complete surgical removal of the tumor. An international study in which MedUni Vienna played a key role provides new evidence that radiotherapy can significantly reduce the recurrence rate. The results, recently published in The Lancet, are set to be incorporated into national and international guidelines.

medical.title: DNA sequencing test finds answers for patients with inherited muscle disease
medical.summary: A test developed by researchers at the Garvan Institute of Medical Research has identified the genetic cause of inherited muscle disease in people who remained without answers after years, sometimes decades, of standard testing. It is the first test of its kind in the world.

medical.title: Higher pollution levels linked to slower marathon times across six World Marathon Majors
medical.summary: A study of more than 2.7 million marathon performances found that higher levels of air pollution on race day were associated with significantly slower finishing times, with recreational runners affected more than elite athletes.

medical.title: Neurotransmitter may help aggressive prostate cancer shut out immune cells from the start
medical.summary: A new study from The Wistar Institute has found a link between the nervous system and the rapid development of neuroendocrine prostate cancer (NEPC), an aggressive form of the disease. Published in Oncogene, the study found high levels of neuromedin U (NMU), a neurotransmitter, in prostate cells during the earliest phase of NEPC formation.

medical.title: Investigating the cost-effectiveness of AI in public health
medical.summary: In the Philippines, public health care remains inaccessible to many because of factors including high costs and the limited availability of medical experts. A new study by Ateneo researchers explores how artificial intelligence (AI) could help address this gap by examining the cost-effectiveness of AI-assisted chest radiograph (X-ray) interpretation.

medical.title: Enzyme USP15 present a promising new target for ovarian cancer treatment
medical.summary: Ovarian cancer is often diagnosed after it has already spread to other parts of the body, at which point the five-year survival rate is under 30%. Further complicating treatment, standard therapies cause substantial harm to healthy cells alongside cancerous ones. But what if ovarian cancer treatment could more specifically target cancerous cells, causing less harm to the rest of the body?

medical.title: Detroit and Flint teens are struggling with their mental health—and worried adults around them feel 'helpless'
medical.summary: Teens in southeast Michigan go to school carrying far more than backpacks, books and water bottles.

medical.title: AI model predicts pancreatic cancer risk 3 years before diagnosis
medical.summary: Researchers at Mayo Clinic have designed an artificial intelligence model that could predict an individual's risk of developing pancreatic cancer years before diagnosis. The research was presented at the American College of Surgeons (ACS) Clinical Congress 2026 in Washington, Sept. 26–29.

medical.title: Urban heat islands linked to worse recovery after major surgery
medical.summary: Patients living in areas with more intense urban heat were less likely to have an optimal recovery after major surgery, according to new research on nearly 700,000 patients.

medical.title: Underweight patients face 92% higher odds of death after emergency general surgery
medical.summary: Underweight patients are more likely to die after emergency general surgery than patients who are normal weight or overweight, and patients who are both frail and underweight face an even higher risk of death and other adverse clinical outcomes, according to new research findings.

medical.title: US will face a shortage of nearly 28,000 surgeons by 2038, first nationwide study finds
medical.summary: The United States will be short by nearly 28,000 surgeons by 2038, according to the first unified assessment of the country's surgical workforce.

science.title: Laser light enables detection of colorectal cancer biomarker in blood within minutes
science.summary: Researchers often use antibodies to detect specific molecules or biological markers because they are remarkably precise at recognizing their targets. However, finding the faint signals of cancer in blood samples is a challenge even for the most reliable techniques.

science.title: New tools pinpoint where urban trees could provide the most relief from heat
science.summary: Cities trying to cool sweltering streets often set broad tree canopy targets. But those targets can overlook the reality that not all shade is equally useful, and not every neighborhood has room for more trees.

science.title: Previously overlooked protein helps cells divide correctly
science.summary: Modern technologies have made it possible to uncover a growing "hidden proteome"—proteins encoded by parts of the genome that researchers previously overlooked. Advances in sequencing and protein analysis are making it possible to find more of these potential proteins and investigate what they do. Researchers at the University of Gothenburg have now identified one such protein.

science.title: Great news from Saturn's moon Enceladus in the search for life in space
science.summary: What are the chances of finding extraterrestrial life in our solar system? Frank Postberg, a professor of planetary science at Freie Universität Berlin, has published a study in Science Advances with an international team of researchers. They present new evidence that it is easier to determine the constituents of the ocean hidden beneath Enceladus's icy surface than previously assumed.

science.title: Plant root injuries unleash pressure waves that travel long distances
science.summary: When plant roots are injured—by insects, for example—the pressure inside the root drops, and a pressure wave spreads rapidly throughout the root system. In neighboring roots, tiny proteins that act as mechanical pressure sensors detect the change and generate electrical and calcium signals.

science.title: Scientists supercharge plant immunity to boost its natural defense response
science.summary: Nanyang Technological University, Singapore (NTU Singapore) scientists have developed a way to "supercharge" a plant's natural immune response.

science.title: Freezing threatens mRNA delivery, but Tris buffer helps nanoparticles retain their potency
science.summary: Researchers at The University of Texas at Austin have teamed up with pharmaceutical company Eli Lilly and Company to uncover how storage conditions affect mRNA lipid nanoparticles (LNPs), the technology behind COVID-19 vaccines and other treatments, and how to make them more effective.

science.title: Testing an antenna layout for the SKA-Low telescope
science.summary: SKA-Low is a radio telescope under construction in Western Australia. It will operate across a wide frequency range, from 50 to 350 MHz, and will be the most sensitive telescope of its kind ever built. The completed instrument will link 512 stations spread across an area roughly 75 km (47 miles) wide. Each station's antennas work together like a single large dish, so their arrangement directly shapes what the telescope can detect.

science.title: Molecular network resource identifies unknown compounds for biomarker discovery
science.summary: Medical researchers, clinicians and pharmaceutical scientists often study small molecules called metabolites, which are produced in living cells through a variety of processes, including the breakdown of food, chemicals or drugs. This area of study is known as metabolomics, and it can be used to identify new signs of disease, measure the effectiveness of medical treatment or study how diet and nutrition affect the body.

science.title: Spin rephasing helps quantum memories store single-photon states longer for future networks
science.summary: We are continuously sending information to each other, transmitting zeros and ones through a giant network of connected computers and devices. Scientists are now trying to extend this familiar concept of the internet to the quantum realm, looking for an efficient way to exchange quantum rather than classical information: qubits instead of bits. The motivation is not just scientific curiosity. Qubits can be a 0, a 1 or any superposition of the two. They can also become entangled, showing a degree of correlation that is out of reach for classical bits.

science.title: Discovery confirms rare, switchable electrical property in widely used electronics material
science.summary: A Husker research team's latest research could open the door to broader use of a class of materials whose electrical properties may someday power next-generation electronics, high-density energy storage, improved computer memory and new strategies for cooling.

science.title: Webb detects ammonia and unexpected chill on a distant giant planet
science.summary: Using the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST), a team of astronomers led by the University of Maryland identified water, methane and ammonia in the atmosphere of HATS-6 b, a giant planet 500 light-years from Earth. The observations also revealed that HATS-6 b may be significantly cooler than standard calculations predict—suggesting that the planet's relationship with its star may be far more complicated than previously thought.

science.title: Students help researchers study how people experience temperature
science.summary: Are there any geographical differences in how people experience weather conditions? This question was investigated in the citizen science project Kallt och svettigt (Cold and sweaty) for a year with the help of school pupils throughout Sweden.

science.title: Private spacecraft falls back to Earth after failing to rescue aging NASA telescope
science.summary: The robotic spacecraft that failed to rescue an aging NASA telescope plunged back to Earth on Friday less than three months after launching on the bold mission.

science.title: Personal experience trumps public reputation when people judge others' refusals
science.summary: A research team led by Professor Hitoshi Yamamoto of Rissho University experimentally examined how people evaluate others when a person's public reputation conflicts with their own experience with that person. The study was published Sept. 14, 2026, in the journal Evolution and Human Behavior.

science.title: Molecular switch-up: Bacteria remodel a peptide to take on new role
science.summary: Remodeling may bring to mind construction crews and scaffolding, but the process is far from unique to buildings. Even molecules can be remodeled. Pandorachelins, newly discovered molecules produced by Pandoraea bacteria, are one example.

science.title: The Uprising: The real medieval revolt that inspired Andrew Garfield's new film
science.summary: The Uprising, a medieval drama directed by Paul Greengrass and starring Andrew Garfield, is set to hit theaters this fall. The film draws its inspiration from the Peasants' Revolt of 1381 in England.

science.title: Researchers track emerging pathogens at Arctic bird gathering
science.summary: Every year, birds migrate north and gather in a single location in the Arctic, and a team of University of Kentucky researchers is collaborating with Alaska Native communities to study how diseases spread and evolve at this gathering before they reach human populations.

science.title: African elephants and medicinal plants: Possible self-medication documented through local ecological knowledge
science.summary: Wild African elephants living in the Mount Elgon region of Kenya appear to seek out specific plants when unwell. Local experts also reported mothers administering plant-based "medicine" to their offspring.

science.title: Trade tensions, high prices and interest rates drive slip in consumers' outlook
science.summary: Consumer sentiment fell by less than four index points in September, reaching its lowest reading in four months and down 15% from January 2026, according to the University of Michigan Surveys of Consumers.

science.title: Two ancient burial sites may explain mystery of Göbeklitepe's scattered human bones
science.summary: Since 1995, archaeologists have excavated hundreds of human bones from Göbeklitepe, an archaeological site in southeastern Türkiye. The ancient remains are around 10,000 years old and date to a time when humans were beginning to settle into permanent farming communities.

science.title: Gen Z communicates differently in the workplace, but older colleagues can still decode them
science.summary: For all the talk about generational differences at work, some of the biggest differences show up in surprisingly ordinary moments.

science.title: 3D images reveal how bacterial cells coordinate protein production and transport across the membrane
science.summary: Scientists have often thought of cells as small, bustling cities with parts that resemble factories, power grids and shipping systems. While past research has illuminated the individual components of these cell cities, scientists haven't had the tools to probe more deeply into how those elements interact.

science.title: Modification of magnetic nanoparticles improves RNA isolation
science.summary: The COVID-19 pandemic clearly demonstrated the importance of rapid and reliable diagnostic methods for detecting and monitoring infectious diseases. Nucleic acids, including RNA, are key biomarkers used in the detection, monitoring and treatment of a wide range of diseases. However, isolating nucleic acids from biological samples can be challenging, particularly when they are present at very low concentrations.

science.title: Climate overshoot will leave lasting impacts even after global temperatures fall
science.summary: Returning global temperatures to a climate target does not necessarily undo the damage caused by exceeding it, new Concordia-led research published in the journal Communications Earth & Environment finds.

environment.title: Ebola, twins and women-led conservation: Reporting on gorillas for World Gorilla Day
environment.summary: Gorillas are among humans’ closest relatives, with a common ancestor dating back around 8 to 10 million years. Both species of gorilla alive today are on the edge of extinction: The eastern gorilla (Gorilla beringei) is listed as endangered on the IUCN Red List, while the western gorilla (Gorilla gorilla) is critically endangered. In its […]

environment.title: In Nepal, women seek ownership rights to the lands they tend
environment.summary: POKHARA, Nepal — Before Binita Bishwokaarma understood Nepal’s property laws, she understood the work required to sustain a farm. Growing up in the village of Sindhupalchok, east of the capital, Kathmandu, she spent much of her time helping her mother around the house and in the fields while her father worked in the city. It’s […]

environment.title: New report reveals the environmental cost of USAID’s destruction
environment.summary: Nearly two years after U.S. President Trump’s decision to dismantle international development agency USAID removed nearly $1 billion from global conservation and environment funding, the agency’s absence is being felt across the world, new analysis says. environment.title: Crocodiles are famous for finding their way home. These ones didn’t
environment.summary: Captive-raised saltwater crocodiles released into Bangladesh’s Sundarbans surprised scientists by settling into the wild rather than trying to return to their breeding facility. The result suggests that releasing larger, mature captive crocodiles could help restore depleted populations more successfully than relying only on vulnerable hatchlings.

environment.title: Back-to-back Arctic storms can double sea ice loss
environment.summary: Scientists have found that Arctic cyclones become especially destructive when several strike one after another. These storm clusters cause about twice as much sea ice loss as isolated cyclones, with impacts that persist roughly two and a half times longer. As Arctic ice becomes thinner and weaker, the damage from these storms appears to be increasing, potentially creating a feedback loop that accelerates future ice loss.

environment.title: Scientists finally see DNA “zip” itself together for the first time
environment.summary: Scientists have directly observed how two negatively charged DNA molecules can pair up despite normally repelling each other. Positively charged metal ions appear to bridge the gap, helping matching DNA helices align groove for groove like a molecular zipper. The discovery confirms a theory proposed two decades ago and could help researchers understand DNA interactions involved in cancer and other cellular processes.

environment.title: Have we found alien life? Hundreds of scientists weigh in
environment.summary: Two major alien-life announcements in 2025 generated enormous excitement, but most astrobiologists remained unconvinced. Only 6.6% of surveyed experts thought possible biological molecules on K2-18b probably represented extraterrestrial life, while 15.1% said the same about intriguing mineral patterns in a Martian rock.

environment.title: Devil’s Arrows: Ancient builders hauled 55,000-pound stones 11 miles for Britain’s tallest stone row
environment.summary: Britain’s towering Devil’s Arrows were built from 25-tonne stones hauled at least 18 kilometers from Brimham Rocks around 4,000 years ago. The discovery reveals an astonishing feat of prehistoric engineering and suggests the stones’ distant source may have been chosen for cultural or spiritual reasons.

environment.title: “Parachute science” is failing the tropics, home to more than 80% of insect species
environment.summary: Insects quietly hold much of the natural world together, yet conservation efforts are overlooking the tropical regions where more than 80 percent of insect species live. Monash University researchers have developed a global framework to close this gap by combining scientific studies with museum collections, local expertise, citizen science, social media records, and new technologies.

environment.title: Geologists reveal the Americas collided millions of years earlier than thought
environment.summary: Volcanic rocks in Colombia are rewriting the timeline of the collision between Central and South America. Their magnetic signatures show that major tectonic deformation had already weakened by the late Miocene, suggesting the most intense collision occurred earlier than previously believed.

mix_items.title: Ce spune directoarea unui cunoscut liceu din București despre reintroducerea uniformei școlare obligatorii
mix_items.summary: Directoarea Colegiului Național „I.L. Caragiale” din București, Andreea Bodea, a declarat vineri, la Digi24, că introducerea uniformelor obligatorii nu va rezolva problema bullying-ului din școli și că o astfel de măsură ar fi greu de aplicat, mai ales în marile orașe. În schimb, ea susține introducerea unui cod vestimentar stabilit de fiecare școală împreună cu elevii și părinții, cu reguli și sancțiuni clare pentru cei care nu îl respectă.

mix_items.title: Laser light enables detection of colorectal cancer biomarker in blood within minutes
mix_items.summary: Researchers often use antibodies to detect specific molecules or biological markers because they are remarkably precise at recognizing their targets. However, finding the faint signals of cancer in blood samples is a challenge even for the most reliable techniques.

mix_items.summary: On the wooded University of Montana campus, resident Cooper's hawks are helping people recover from stroke.

mix_items.summary: Cities trying to cool sweltering streets often set broad tree canopy targets. But those targets can overlook the reality that not all shade is equally useful, and not every neighborhood has room for more trees.

mix_items.title: Previously overlooked protein helps cells divide correctly
mix_items.summary: Modern technologies have made it possible to uncover a growing "hidden proteome"—proteins encoded by parts of the genome that researchers previously overlooked. Advances in sequencing and protein analysis are making it possible to find more of these potential proteins and investigate what they do. Researchers at the University of Gothenburg have now identified one such protein.

mix_items.title: Years of fine-particle pollution track with childhood ADHD rates across US counties
mix_items.summary: Air quality across the country has improved greatly over the decades, as shown in Environmental Protection Agency reports. These improvements are good news overall, but lingering effects of past air pollution still raise health concerns for many people. UT researchers Alex Bentley and Larisa Ozeryansky co-authored a paper published in September in Scientific Reports. It explores the strong association between measures of fine-particulate air pollution (called PM 2.5) in the United States and the prevalence of attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) in children years later.

mix_items.title: Adding neurons may keep improving visual signals despite shared noise, analysis predicts
mix_items.summary: Our brains internally represent the outside world through the coordinated activity of billions of neurons. A single neuron responds unreliably: Even when the same stimulus is shown repeatedly, its activity varies from trial to trial. Neuron populations can compensate for this variability by representing the same information across many neurons, a strategy known as population coding.

mix_items.title: Great news from Saturn's moon Enceladus in the search for life in space
mix_items.summary: What are the chances of finding extraterrestrial life in our solar system? Frank Postberg, a professor of planetary science at Freie Universität Berlin, has published a study in Science Advances with an international team of researchers. They present new evidence that it is easier to determine the constituents of the ocean hidden beneath Enceladus's icy surface than previously assumed.

mix_items.title: Plant root injuries unleash pressure waves that travel long distances
mix_items.summary: When plant roots are injured—by insects, for example—the pressure inside the root drops, and a pressure wave spreads rapidly throughout the root system. In neighboring roots, tiny proteins that act as mechanical pressure sensors detect the change and generate electrical and calcium signals.

mix_items.title: What is trauma‑informed care—and how do schools do it?
mix_items.summary: Trauma-informed approaches have become increasingly prominent in education policy and guidance, although the term is not always explicitly used.

mix_items.title: Scientists supercharge plant immunity to boost its natural defense response
mix_items.summary: Nanyang Technological University, Singapore (NTU Singapore) scientists have developed a way to "supercharge" a plant's natural immune response.

mix_items.title: Hidden E. coli survive in bladder cells, but existing drug helps antibiotics reach them in lab tests
mix_items.summary: Urinary tract infections, or UTIs, are among the most common bacterial infections and are caused mostly by the uropathogenic bacterium Escherichia coli. But even after antibiotic treatment, many patients experience another UTI.

mix_items.title: New brain tumor test could transform diagnosis and treatment
mix_items.summary: Scientists and doctors at Newcastle are among the first in the U.K. to use a pioneering brain tumor test with the potential to speed up diagnosis for patients—from weeks to hours.

mix_items.title: Freezing threatens mRNA delivery, but Tris buffer helps nanoparticles retain their potency
mix_items.summary: Researchers at The University of Texas at Austin have teamed up with pharmaceutical company Eli Lilly and Company to uncover how storage conditions affect mRNA lipid nanoparticles (LNPs), the technology behind COVID-19 vaccines and other treatments, and how to make them more effective.

mix_items.title: Dietary supplement may influence lung tumor growth differently in females and males
mix_items.summary: A study led by researchers at the UCLA Health Jonsson Comprehensive Cancer Center found that a dietary form of a naturally occurring molecule called calcium alpha-ketoglutarate, or Ca-αKG, reduced lung tumor growth in female mice and activated genes associated with better outcomes in women with lung cancer. The researchers also found that Ca-αKG had the opposite effect in male mice, where it was associated with larger tumors and increased tumor-cell proliferation.

mix_items.title: Testing an antenna layout for the SKA-Low telescope
mix_items.summary: SKA-Low is a radio telescope under construction in Western Australia. It will operate across a wide frequency range, from 50 to 350 MHz, and will be the most sensitive telescope of its kind ever built. The completed instrument will link 512 stations spread across an area roughly 75 km (47 miles) wide. Each station's antennas work together like a single large dish, so their arrangement directly shapes what the telescope can detect.

mix_items.title: Molecular network resource identifies unknown compounds for biomarker discovery
mix_items.summary: Medical researchers, clinicians and pharmaceutical scientists often study small molecules called metabolites, which are produced in living cells through a variety of processes, including the breakdown of food, chemicals or drugs. This area of study is known as metabolomics, and it can be used to identify new signs of disease, measure the effectiveness of medical treatment or study how diet and nutrition affect the body.

mix_items.title: Migraine and sleep are strongly interconnected, study finds
mix_items.summary: Sleep problems are significantly more common among people with migraine than among those without headaches. People with migraine also tend to have a later chronotype, meaning they tend to fall asleep and wake up later and are most active later in the day.

mix_items.title: A brainstem signal reorganizes the neural code for taste
mix_items.summary: Why might food seem appealing in one state of mind and less enticing in another? New UConn research offers insight into how the brain systems that regulate alertness and stress may reshape how taste is represented in the brain.

mix_items.title: Spin rephasing helps quantum memories store single-photon states longer for future networks
mix_items.summary: We are continuously sending information to each other, transmitting zeros and ones through a giant network of connected computers and devices. Scientists are now trying to extend this familiar concept of the internet to the quantum realm, looking for an efficient way to exchange quantum rather than classical information: qubits instead of bits. The motivation is not just scientific curiosity. Qubits can be a 0, a 1 or any superposition of the two. They can also become entangled, showing a degree of correlation that is out of reach for classical bits.

mix_items.title: CDC vaccine policy recommendations grind to a halt under Health Secretary Kennedy
mix_items.summary: The Food and Drug Administration recently approved a new flu vaccine that tested well in older adults. But the federal agency responsible for telling doctors and the general public how to use it has made no recommendation on it.

mix_items.title: Study identifies two factors that may help patients benefit from off-the-shelf CAR T-cell therapies
mix_items.summary: Researchers at The University of Texas MD Anderson Cancer Center have traced how off-the-shelf chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T cells behave in patients, revealing how immune rejection and differences among CAR T cells influence their ability to multiply after infusion.

mix_items.title: Discovery confirms rare, switchable electrical property in widely used electronics material
mix_items.summary: A Husker research team's latest research could open the door to broader use of a class of materials whose electrical properties may someday power next-generation electronics, high-density energy storage, improved computer memory and new strategies for cooling.

mix_items.title: UACR, UPCR provide indistinguishable prognostic information in chronic kidney disease
mix_items.summary: In a cohort of patients with chronic kidney disease (CKD), urinary albumin-creatinine ratio (UACR) and urinary protein-creatinine ratio (UPCR) provide clinically indistinguishable prognostic information for kidney and cardiovascular outcomes, according to a research letter published online Sept. 23 in the Journal of the American Medical Association.

mix_items.title: Radiotherapy after surgery significantly reduces atypical meningioma recurrence, clinical trial finds
mix_items.summary: Atypical meningiomas are tumors that originate in the meninges and are associated with a high risk of recurrence. Until now, it was unclear whether patients benefit from radiotherapy after complete surgical removal of the tumor. An international study in which MedUni Vienna played a key role provides new evidence that radiotherapy can significantly reduce the recurrence rate. The results, recently published in The Lancet, are set to be incorporated into national and international guidelines.

mix_items.title: Webb detects ammonia and unexpected chill on a distant giant planet
mix_items.summary: Using the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST), a team of astronomers led by the University of Maryland identified water, methane and ammonia in the atmosphere of HATS-6 b, a giant planet 500 light-years from Earth. The observations also revealed that HATS-6 b may be significantly cooler than standard calculations predict—suggesting that the planet's relationship with its star may be far more complicated than previously thought.

mix_items.title: Students help researchers study how people experience temperature
mix_items.summary: Are there any geographical differences in how people experience weather conditions? This question was investigated in the citizen science project Kallt och svettigt (Cold and sweaty) for a year with the help of school pupils throughout Sweden.

mix_items.title: Private spacecraft falls back to Earth after failing to rescue aging NASA telescope
mix_items.summary: The robotic spacecraft that failed to rescue an aging NASA telescope plunged back to Earth on Friday less than three months after launching on the bold mission.

mix_items.title: Personal experience trumps public reputation when people judge others' refusals
mix_items.summary: A research team led by Professor Hitoshi Yamamoto of Rissho University experimentally examined how people evaluate others when a person's public reputation conflicts with their own experience with that person. The study was published Sept. 14, 2026, in the journal Evolution and Human Behavior.

mix_items.title: Molecular switch-up: Bacteria remodel a peptide to take on new role
mix_items.summary: Remodeling may bring to mind construction crews and scaffolding, but the process is far from unique to buildings. Even molecules can be remodeled. Pandorachelins, newly discovered molecules produced by Pandoraea bacteria, are one example.

mix_items.title: The Uprising: The real medieval revolt that inspired Andrew Garfield's new film
mix_items.summary: The Uprising, a medieval drama directed by Paul Greengrass and starring Andrew Garfield, is set to hit theaters this fall. The film draws its inspiration from the Peasants' Revolt of 1381 in England.

mix_items.title: DNA sequencing test finds answers for patients with inherited muscle disease
mix_items.summary: A test developed by researchers at the Garvan Institute of Medical Research has identified the genetic cause of inherited muscle disease in people who remained without answers after years, sometimes decades, of standard testing. It is the first test of its kind in the world.

mix_items.title: Higher pollution levels linked to slower marathon times across six World Marathon Majors
mix_items.summary: A study of more than 2.7 million marathon performances found that higher levels of air pollution on race day were associated with significantly slower finishing times, with recreational runners affected more than elite athletes.

mix_items.title: Neurotransmitter may help aggressive prostate cancer shut out immune cells from the start
mix_items.summary: A new study from The Wistar Institute has found a link between the nervous system and the rapid development of neuroendocrine prostate cancer (NEPC), an aggressive form of the disease. Published in Oncogene, the study found high levels of neuromedin U (NMU), a neurotransmitter, in prostate cells during the earliest phase of NEPC formation.

mix_items.title: Researchers track emerging pathogens at Arctic bird gathering
mix_items.summary: Every year, birds migrate north and gather in a single location in the Arctic, and a team of University of Kentucky researchers is collaborating with Alaska Native communities to study how diseases spread and evolve at this gathering before they reach human populations.

mix_items.title: Investigating the cost-effectiveness of AI in public health
mix_items.summary: In the Philippines, public health care remains inaccessible to many because of factors including high costs and the limited availability of medical experts. A new study by Ateneo researchers explores how artificial intelligence (AI) could help address this gap by examining the cost-effectiveness of AI-assisted chest radiograph (X-ray) interpretation.

mix_items.title: African elephants and medicinal plants: Possible self-medication documented through local ecological knowledge
mix_items.summary: Wild African elephants living in the Mount Elgon region of Kenya appear to seek out specific plants when unwell. Local experts also reported mothers administering plant-based "medicine" to their offspring.

mix_items.title: Trade tensions, high prices and interest rates drive slip in consumers' outlook
mix_items.summary: Consumer sentiment fell by less than four index points in September, reaching its lowest reading in four months and down 15% from January 2026, according to the University of Michigan Surveys of Consumers.

mix_items.title: Enzyme USP15 present a promising new target for ovarian cancer treatment
mix_items.summary: Ovarian cancer is often diagnosed after it has already spread to other parts of the body, at which point the five-year survival rate is under 30%. Further complicating treatment, standard therapies cause substantial harm to healthy cells alongside cancerous ones. But what if ovarian cancer treatment could more specifically target cancerous cells, causing less harm to the rest of the body?

mix_items.title: Detroit and Flint teens are struggling with their mental health—and worried adults around them feel 'helpless'
mix_items.summary: Teens in southeast Michigan go to school carrying far more than backpacks, books and water bottles.

mix_items.title: Two ancient burial sites may explain mystery of Göbeklitepe's scattered human bones
mix_items.summary: Since 1995, archaeologists have excavated hundreds of human bones from Göbeklitepe, an archaeological site in southeastern Türkiye. The ancient remains are around 10,000 years old and date to a time when humans were beginning to settle into permanent farming communities.

mix_items.title: AI model predicts pancreatic cancer risk 3 years before diagnosis
mix_items.summary: Researchers at Mayo Clinic have designed an artificial intelligence model that could predict an individual's risk of developing pancreatic cancer years before diagnosis. The research was presented at the American College of Surgeons (ACS) Clinical Congress 2026 in Washington, Sept. 26–29.

mix_items.title: Gen Z communicates differently in the workplace, but older colleagues can still decode them
mix_items.summary: For all the talk about generational differences at work, some of the biggest differences show up in surprisingly ordinary moments.

mix_items.title: Urban heat islands linked to worse recovery after major surgery
mix_items.summary: Patients living in areas with more intense urban heat were less likely to have an optimal recovery after major surgery, according to new research on nearly 700,000 patients.

mix_items.title: Underweight patients face 92% higher odds of death after emergency general surgery
mix_items.summary: Underweight patients are more likely to die after emergency general surgery than patients who are normal weight or overweight, and patients who are both frail and underweight face an even higher risk of death and other adverse clinical outcomes, according to new research findings.

mix_items.title: US will face a shortage of nearly 28,000 surgeons by 2038, first nationwide study finds
mix_items.summary: The United States will be short by nearly 28,000 surgeons by 2038, according to the first unified assessment of the country's surgical workforce.

mix_items.title: 3D images reveal how bacterial cells coordinate protein production and transport across the membrane
mix_items.summary: Scientists have often thought of cells as small, bustling cities with parts that resemble factories, power grids and shipping systems. While past research has illuminated the individual components of these cell cities, scientists haven't had the tools to probe more deeply into how those elements interact.

mix_items.title: Modification of magnetic nanoparticles improves RNA isolation
mix_items.summary: The COVID-19 pandemic clearly demonstrated the importance of rapid and reliable diagnostic methods for detecting and monitoring infectious diseases. Nucleic acids, including RNA, are key biomarkers used in the detection, monitoring and treatment of a wide range of diseases. However, isolating nucleic acids from biological samples can be challenging, particularly when they are present at very low concentrations.

mix_items.title: Climate overshoot will leave lasting impacts even after global temperatures fall
mix_items.summary: Returning global temperatures to a climate target does not necessarily undo the damage caused by exceeding it, new Concordia-led research published in the journal Communications Earth & Environment finds.

mix_items.title: Ebola, twins and women-led conservation: Reporting on gorillas for World Gorilla Day
mix_items.summary: Gorillas are among humans’ closest relatives, with a common ancestor dating back around 8 to 10 million years. Both species of gorilla alive today are on the edge of extinction: The eastern gorilla (Gorilla beringei) is listed as endangered on the IUCN Red List, while the western gorilla (Gorilla gorilla) is critically endangered. In its […]

mix_items.title: In Nepal, women seek ownership rights to the lands they tend
mix_items.summary: POKHARA, Nepal — Before Binita Bishwokaarma understood Nepal’s property laws, she understood the work required to sustain a farm. Growing up in the village of Sindhupalchok, east of the capital, Kathmandu, she spent much of her time helping her mother around the house and in the fields while her father worked in the city. It’s […]

mix_items.title: New report reveals the environmental cost of USAID’s destruction
mix_items.summary: Nearly two years after U.S. President Trump’s decision to dismantle international development agency USAID removed nearly $1 billion from global conservation and environment funding, the agency’s absence is being felt across the world, new analysis says. The abrupt termination of around 5,200 contracts in early 2025 ended support for activities as varied as plastic waste […]

mix_items.title: ‘Lost’ bird reappears in West Africa’s forests after more than a decade
mix_items.summary: When Paulo Ditzel first laid eyes on the bird, he knew he’d seen something special: a vibrant orange body with yellow and black wings and tail feathers, topped by a dark head set off by almost-whimsical splashes of copper on its cheek. “My brain registered, it’s the Ghana cuckooshrike,” Ditzel, a field research fellow with […]

mix_items.title: Biodiversity credits shouldn’t copy the carbon market playbook (commentary)
mix_items.summary: Here is the argument I want to make plainly, before anything else: the biodiversity credit market should stop trying to copy carbon’s trick of reducing everything to one tradable unit, and should instead measure its own success by how continuously and independently a claim can be verified. Chasing a single elegant number, the way carbon […]

mix_items.title: Crocodiles are famous for finding their way home. These ones didn’t
mix_items.summary: Captive-raised saltwater crocodiles released into Bangladesh’s Sundarbans surprised scientists by settling into the wild rather than trying to return to their breeding facility. The result suggests that releasing larger, mature captive crocodiles could help restore depleted populations more successfully than relying only on vulnerable hatchlings.

mix_items.title: Back-to-back Arctic storms can double sea ice loss
mix_items.summary: Scientists have found that Arctic cyclones become especially destructive when several strike one after another. These storm clusters cause about twice as much sea ice loss as isolated cyclones, with impacts that persist roughly two and a half times longer. As Arctic ice becomes thinner and weaker, the damage from these storms appears to be increasing, potentially creating a feedback loop that accelerates future ice loss.

mix_items.title: Scientists finally see DNA “zip” itself together for the first time
mix_items.summary: Scientists have directly observed how two negatively charged DNA molecules can pair up despite normally repelling each other. Positively charged metal ions appear to bridge the gap, helping matching DNA helices align groove for groove like a molecular zipper. The discovery confirms a theory proposed two decades ago and could help researchers understand DNA interactions involved in cancer and other cellular processes.

mix_items.title: Have we found alien life? Hundreds of scientists weigh in
mix_items.summary: Two major alien-life announcements in 2025 generated enormous excitement, but most astrobiologists remained unconvinced. Only 6.6% of surveyed experts thought possible biological molecules on K2-18b probably represented extraterrestrial life, while 15.1% said the same about intriguing mineral patterns in a Martian rock.

mix_items.title: Devil’s Arrows: Ancient builders hauled 55,000-pound stones 11 miles for Britain’s tallest stone row
mix_items.summary: Britain’s towering Devil’s Arrows were built from 25-tonne stones hauled at least 18 kilometers from Brimham Rocks around 4,000 years ago. The discovery reveals an astonishing feat of prehistoric engineering and suggests the stones’ distant source may have been chosen for cultural or spiritual reasons.

mix_items.title: “Parachute science” is failing the tropics, home to more than 80% of insect species
mix_items.summary: Insects quietly hold much of the natural world together, yet conservation efforts are overlooking the tropical regions where more than 80 percent of insect species live. Monash University researchers have developed a global framework to close this gap by combining scientific studies with museum collections, local expertise, citizen science, social media records, and new technologies.

mix_items.title: Geologists reveal the Americas collided millions of years earlier than thought
mix_items.summary: Volcanic rocks in Colombia are rewriting the timeline of the collision between Central and South America. Their magnetic signatures show that major tectonic deformation had already weakened by the late Miocene, suggesting the most intense collision occurred earlier than previously believed.

mix_items.title: A Trio of Tropical Cyclones in the Pacific
mix_items.summary: The Pacific was buzzing with storms while the Atlantic was notably quiet. The post A Trio of Tropical Cyclones in the Pacific appeared first on NASA Science .
